questions.enonce_markdown:
Why was the Gospel of John written?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Gospel gives its own statement of purpose: "these are written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name" (John 20:30-31). Beyond this, scholars suggest further aims connected with the situation of the community in which the Gospel was written. This answer considers the stated purpose and the other proposed purposes.

**1. To bring people to faith (evangelistic).** The key words "believe" and "life" appear throughout the Gospel. The signs are selected to lead readers to faith in Jesus as Messiah and Son of God (John 2:11; 20:30). Some interpret this as an appeal to non-believing Jews and Greeks; others read the verb as "continue to believe" and see the Gospel written to strengthen those who already believe.

**2. To answer Jewish opposition.** The Gospel reflects a conflict with the synagogue. It speaks of believers being put out of the synagogue (John 9:22; 12:42; 16:2). The long debates with "the Jews" over the Sabbath, over Moses and over the identity of Jesus (John 5-10) defend the claim that Jesus fulfils the Law and the Scriptures (John 5:39, 46).

**3. To correct the followers of John the Baptist.** The Gospel repeatedly states that John the Baptist was not the light but a witness to it (John 1:6-8, 19-27; 3:22-30). This may answer groups who regarded John as the Messiah.

**4. To oppose false teaching about Christ.** The statement that "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14) emphasises the real humanity of Jesus, perhaps against early views which denied that the Son of God truly became a man. The Gospel also strongly affirms his divinity (John 1:1; 20:28), against those who regarded him as merely human.

**5. To supplement the other Gospels.** John gives material not found in the Synoptics, for example the wedding at Cana, Nicodemus, the raising of Lazarus and the farewell discourses, and so may have been written to fill out and interpret the story of Jesus.

**6. To encourage and instruct the Christian community.** The Farewell Discourses (John 13-17) speak of the Spirit, of love and of unity, and prepare the believers to live after the departure of Jesus. The clarification that the beloved disciple was not promised to live until the return of Christ (John 21:22-23) shows a concern with the community's questions.

**Conclusion.** The Gospel was written primarily so that readers would believe and have life, and the stated purpose is the most secure one. The other purposes, concerning the synagogue, John the Baptist's followers, false teaching and the needs of the church, are suggested by hints in the text and need not exclude each other.
